title: The Monday that got away
text:
Ivan opened his laptop at 8:15 with a clear plan. Finish the client proposal, follow up on two invoices, and call it a day by six.

At 8:40 his manager sent a message: "Quick heads up, the client moved the meeting to Wednesday." Two days earlier than planned. Ivan looked at the half-finished proposal and felt his stomach drop.

He decided to take the lead instead of panicking. He wrote to the designer: "Can I run something by you? I need the cover page by tomorrow morning, not Thursday." She replied in four minutes: "No problem, I have the bandwidth today."

Then he did the harder thing. He emailed the client and asked one direct question: which three sections mattered most to them. The answer came back within the hour, and two of the sections he had been polishing were not on the list.

By five o'clock the proposal was done, shorter than planned and better than the original. The invoices, though, were still sitting there. Ivan added them to Tuesday and closed the laptop.

He didn't finish everything. He finished the thing that moved the needle.

options: The client moved the meeting earlier
His manager gave him a new project
The designer was unavailable
He lost the proposal file

questions.q: What did the designer mean by "I have the bandwidth today"?
options: She had time and energy to help
She needed a faster internet connection
She was too busy to help
She wanted to work from home

questions.q: What was the result of Ivan's email to the client?
options: He learned two sections weren't needed
The client cancelled the meeting
The client asked for more sections
The client complained about the delay

questions.q: What does the last line suggest about Ivan's day?
options: He prioritised the work that mattered most
He wasted the whole day
He finished every task on his list
He asked his manager for help

title: The meeting nobody needed
text:
Every Thursday at ten, eleven people joined a call that lasted an hour. Nobody had put it in the calendar recently. It had simply always been there.

The new team lead, Dana, watched it twice and noticed something. In sixty minutes, roughly nine of them were useful. The rest was people repeating updates that were already written down.

At the third meeting she brought it up. "I want to be on the same page before I change anything," she said. "Does this meeting help you?" Silence, then one person spoke up: "Honestly, I get sidetracked for the rest of the morning after it."

Dana didn't cancel the meeting. She cut it to fifteen minutes, made everyone send written updates the day before, and kept the call for one thing only: decisions that were up in the air.

The first short version felt strange. The second one ran nine minutes. By the fourth week, two people said it was the only meeting they didn't dread.

Dana later said the change was easy. Asking the question in front of everyone was the hard part.

questions.q: What did Dana notice about the meeting?
options: Most of the hour was not useful
Too few people attended
It was scheduled at a bad time
Nobody prepared for it

questions.q: What did the team member mean by "I get sidetracked"?
options: He loses focus afterwards
He forgets the meeting
He enjoys the discussion
He arrives late
Shortened it and moved updates to writing
Cancelled the meeting completely
Invited more people to join
Moved it to a different day

questions.q: According to Dana, what was the difficult part?
options: Asking the question openly
Writing the new agenda
Convincing her manager
Learning the new software
